summary: In Greek mythology, Eurytus (Ancient Greek: Εὔρυτος) was one of the Giants (Gigantes), earthborn opponents of the Olympian gods in the Gigantomachy. Apollodorus says Dionysus killed him with a thyrsus. He is distinct from the Oechalian king, the Argonaut son of Hermes, and other figures who share the name.

sections.heading: Identity
paragraphs: Eurytus appears in the catalogue of Giants who fought the Olympians. In the Hesiodic tradition the Giants are offspring of Gaia born from the blood of castrated Uranus. Later mythographers give individual Giants names and opponents; Apollodorus names Eurytus among those destroyed in the Gigantomachy.

sections.heading: Mythology
paragraphs: According to Apollodorus (Bibliotheca 1.6.2), during the Gigantomachy Eurytus was killed by Dionysus with his thyrsus. Other Giants in the same narrative fall to Apollo and Heracles, Hecate, Hephaestus, Athena, Poseidon, Hermes, Artemis, and the Moirai, among others; Zeus finishes the rest with thunderbolts while Heracles shoots them as they die.
Beyond this battle-roll notice Eurytus has little separate myth; his place is as a named combatant in the war of the earthborn against the gods.

sections.heading: Homonyms
paragraphs: This atlas entry (eurytus-giant) is the earthborn Giant of the Gigantomachy. Distinct from Eurytus king of Oechalia (eurytus-oechalia), father of Iole; from the Argonaut Eurytus (or Erytus) son of Hermes (eurytus-hermes); from the Epeian leader at Troy (eurytus-epeian); and from other minor figures listed on the Wikipedia disambiguation page Eurytus.
